content.content:
# Cold read of the climb-batch-29 orientation

Read: `CLAUDE.md`, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md` (the core), and `orientation.md` (121 lines) in this folder. Nothing else was opened. Line numbers are those of `orientation.md`. "Core" means `SKILL.md`.

## 1. What I would do differently, section by section

### Preamble (lines 1-7)

- Take each bold sentence as this tree's rule over the specification, a team test, an old note or my training. Question one only with evidence that its decision did not use. Limit: a sentence with no P-N can be built on but not cited as a curator decision.
- Cite a sentence that names P-N as a decision of the curator.
- Never write a test that asserts as correct a behaviour that a sentence ties to a ledger row. Limit: the file does not say what the test should assert instead, for example the bold rule marked as an `XXX` expected failure.
- Leave a limit that opens "Until the switch-over" unfixed in the compiler's prelude, and keep such code out of compiled tests. Limit: the core says the prelude is three files of the compiler's library, and the file does not say whether its other files are off limits too (2.8).
- Before I call a disagreement a conflict, search FACTS and POSITIONS.
- Drop three priors even when an old note or a team test supports them: the number types nest, fixed-width arithmetic wraps, and walk passes arguments without converting them.
- Do not cite `Specification-1.0-frozen/` (the Working Draft) as the specification. Look in Appendix I for the text that a rule replaced.

### Dispatch and overloading (lines 9-24)

- Accept overloads that differ only in their static-parameter bounds (P-45). Check that the more specific one's return type is a subtype of the other's at every instance.
- Judge exclusion between generic overloads over the whole parameter tuple. A generic type shared at one position, such as `Box[\T\]` in both, forces equal static arguments. A parameter that nothing ties, such as `U` against `T`, means both paths refuse the pair. Limit: P-157's substitution of the bounds' meet is stated for the checker only (2.16).
- Never rely on declaration order under walk. Read "Cannot unify" as an argument outside the bound of a trait's generic method.
- Never take walk's loading of a program as proof that it is valid, and never change code only to pass walk's load check. Look up `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", first.
- Never declare two functional methods with equivalent parameter types and `self` in different positions. Never put an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait. When an object inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, declare the method in the object, even though Scala would not ask for it (P-149).
- Give a program's trait that declares its own functional `+`, `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` an `excludes { Number }` or an `excludes { HasRank }`, or move the operator into an object. Otherwise expect "fails the Meet Rule" under walk. Never take a compiled success as proof (row 918). Limit: line 43 seems to exempt self-typed traits (2.2).

### Traits and objects (lines 26-62)

- Never write a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Never copy a specification example marked "Not allowed". Expect walk to refuse overloads on `Tg[\3\]` and `Tg[\4\]` (row 416).
- Do not list every subtype in a `comprises` clause. Do not trust walk's load check of extenders outside the main component (row 551).
- Never write a Java-style `override` at the inherited parameter types: declare the method again without `override`. In the library such an `override` stops every program. Use `override` only to widen. Limits: the code generator refuses every `override` (row 650), so no compiled test can carry one, and the checker accepts the Java-style form (row 653). The file does not say what a widening `override` does at dispatch (2.14).
- To implement an inherited abstract method in an object, give it one body or several narrower bodies that cover its parameter types, reading `comprises` clauses. Avoid a cover by several bodies where the checker runs and any of the methods has static parameters (row 725). Do not expect walk to check a generic object (row 665).
- In a self-typed trait, use `self` as the implementing type without a cast. Never extend `T[\A\]` from a type that is not an `A`. Keep a body that returns `self` out of compiled code (row 695). Expect walk's load check to refuse such a trait's operator beside the library's array-number one in the two listed cases.
- Bound an index parameter by `Index`, but only in code that runs under walk or is checked against the interpreter's library, never in a compiled program before the switch-over. Pass `m[i, j]` as one tuple index. In checked code, take a tuple index at `I extends Index`, not at `Index` (row 805). Do not treat `()` as an index.
- Order tuples only when every element type extends `StandardPartialOrder`. Under walk, never compare numbers of two run-time types at one position (row 511). In checked code, never order a `List[\RR64\]`.
- Assume `=` is `SEQV` on a type that declares no `=`, so strings compare by identity there. Give a value object that holds strings its own `=`. For equivalence of booleans write `<->`, never `EQV` or `≡`. Expect tuples longer than three to fall back to `SEQV`. Before the switch-over, a compiled `===` compares by `=` (row 908).

### Static parameters, `where` clauses and sizes (lines 64-83)

- Expect a type parameter that a call does not fix to take its bound. Under walk, write the static argument wherever the checker would take it from the enclosing call, as `mk[\ZZ64\]()` (row 705). Expect `Bottom` in the three listed cases.
- Write a conditional extension only as `extends P where { T extends X }`. Expect the checker to ignore any other `where` on an `extends` entry without a message. Never rely on either run time to honour a conditional extension or a method's `where` condition. Keep a function with `where [\nat n\]` out of compiled programs (row 867).
- Treat two sizes as equal only when they are written alike after numeral arithmetic, so `s0 s1` is not `s1 s0`. Do not assume an arm on `N[\0\]` is unreachable. Keep size powers non-negative and at most 4096, except for 0, 1 and -1.
- Use `reflect` from `NatReflect` only under walk, now and after the switch-over. In compiled code, never pass a value of a trait whose `comprises` lists a type at a `where`-clause size where that listed type is expected (row 307).

### Numbers (lines 85-103)

- Read "route A", "route C" and "the tower" in the record as names. None of them means that the number types nest.
- Rely on a numeral converting at a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter or a declared return type. Expect the default everywhere else, and never move a defaulted value into another type (`q: QQ = x`). Read a `nat` or `int` parameter's value as a `ZZ32` (2.1).
- Never use `NaturalNumeral` or `RadixPointNumeral` as the type of a variable, a field or a return. Give my own number type a `coerce` from each. Expect `array1` and `array2` to give a plain array at that type.
- In a test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation, bind a typed operand first: an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`2147483647 + 1` does not overflow).
- Expect a generic call to promote to the narrowest common coercion target, but under walk not across the elements of a tuple or varargs (rows 395, 511). Expect "Ambiguous coercion" when overloads apply only by coercion.
- Convert integers with an `asZZ32`-style getter when a value must be checked, and with `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` or `big` when wrapping is wanted. For a `ZZ`, use the getters. Before the switch-over, expect the compiled prelude to have only the listed getters (row 349).
- Never write arithmetic generic over `T extends Number`: declare it once per number type. Never compare across number types with `=` unless a coercion exists between them, because a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64` is silently `false`. Use `asFloat`.
- Expect `^` to answer its base's type and to raise at a negative exponent. Write `2.0^(-1)` or a `QQ` base. Keep integer powers out of compiled code beyond the listed types (rows 441, 523).
- Expect `/` on integers to give a `QQ`. Truncate with `DIV`. Get a float with `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` operands, or with `asFloat` for `ZZ64` ones. Never write integer `/` in compiled code before the switch-over.

### Reductions and comprehensions (lines 105-115)

- Write the static argument in every clause form of `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN` (row 731). For other reductions under walk, declare the type at a local variable or at a function's return. A method's return type, a field, a parameter or an assignment does not direct it.
- Never assert walk's empty untyped `SUM` (row 716). Never give `SUM` a static argument that is not a number type (row 436).
- Declare `simpleJoin` at `R` in my own reduction without an identity, and never copy the team tests' `Any` or untyped form.

### Implementation limits (lines 117-121)

- Never write a `Maybe` as an `if` condition.
- Write the type of every parameter of a function, method or local function. Limit: the file does not say whether a function expression is covered (2.13).
- Let a component's function take its return type from its api, or write the type when the api has none or several declarations at those parameter types.

## 2. Passages that would send a worker wrong, read two ways, or use a term the core does not give

2.1 Line 89 against the core. Line 89 says "A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-40)". The core, "Fortress as a language", says "sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`)". A worker who read the core first writes `u: NN32 = n`. If the core means that the kind ranges over `NN32` values while the value is typed `ZZ32`, one of the two files must say so. Confidence high (75%).

2.2 Line 24 against line 43. Line 24: a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's array-number `+`, and walk refuses it with "fails the Meet Rule" unless the trait excludes `Number` or `HasRank`. Line 43: with P-157's reading, walk "loads such a pair in the library and in a program's own component", except in two cases. For a program's self-typed trait, such as `trait Vec[\V extends Vec[\V\]\]` with `opr +(self, o: V)`, I cannot tell whether I must add the `excludes`. "Such a pair in a program's own component" also reads two ways: the program's trait against the library's `+`, or both declarations inside the program. Confidence medium-high (65%).

2.3 Line 7's convention against the rest of the file. Line 7 says that a sentence citing a ledger row states a departure, and that a sentence without one can be built on. Several departures cite no row, so a worker would take them as rules and assert them in tests:
- line 43, walk's load check refusing a valid pair in the two listed cases;
- line 66, a type holding `OPEN` admitting "only what it admits at `Bottom`";
- line 79, "the code generator ... emits no code for it, so the compiled runtime does not check it";
- line 81, "Walk refuses a negative exponent", which is a rule or a departure.
Going the other way, line 62 cites row 923 as "the question of longer tuples". That row holds an open question, not a departure, so I cannot tell whether `(s, 1, 2, 3) = (t, 1, 2, 3)` being `false` may be asserted. Confidence medium-high (70%).

2.4 Line 95, numerals between overloads. "Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: 'Ambiguous coercion'. Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`". Taken literally, walk stops on `f(3)` beside `f(x: ZZ32)` and `f(x: RR64)`, the commonest case of all. The other reading is that under walk the numeral is already a `ZZ32` when it runs, so `f(ZZ32)` fits without a coercion. The file does not say what a numeral is at run time under walk. Confidence medium (55%).

2.5 Line 66, the `pick` example. `pick(x: (T,T))` does not show `T`'s bound. The behaviour applies only to a parameter "whose bound names itself", so with `T` unbounded the example does not show the rule. "A type that holds `OPEN`" also reads two ways against "Every value passes `OPEN` itself": I cannot tell whether a bare `pick(x: T)` beside `pick(x: Any)` takes every value or none. "Where walk compares overloads", at load or at the call, is also open. Confidence medium (55%).

2.6 Lines 89, 62 and 93: `=` as binding and as equality. In line 89, `u: NN32 = 5` and `n = 3000000000` bind, while "`h = 0.5` is `true`" compares. The core teaches that "`x = e` declares an immutable variable", so a reader new to Fortress takes `h = 0.5` as rebinding `h`. Writing "`(h = 0.5)` evaluates to `true`" would remove the doubt. Confidence medium (55%).

2.7 Lines 89, 93 and 103: the default of a folded non-integer. Line 89's defaults are `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` or `ZZ`, and `RR64` with a radix point. Line 93 says "`7/2` is a `QQ`", and line 103 says "`7 / 2` is `7/2`". The fold's result is "one numeral, which converts or takes its default", and the default list has no case for a value that is not an integer and has no radix point. So the type of `x = 7/2` comes only from the example. Confidence medium (55%).

2.8 Lines 7, 48, 89, 97 and 101: "compiler's prelude" against "compiler's library". The core defines the prelude as three files of the compiler's library. The file uses both names for limits that end at the switch-over, and forbids fixes only "in the compiler's prelude". I cannot tell whether a fix in the compiler's other library files is allowed, or whether the two names mean the same thing here. Confidence medium-low (45%).

2.9 Line 93 against the core. The core says that `fortress compile` "folds integer literals" before the checker. Line 93 says that every expression of numerals alone folds, comparisons and powers and string `||` included, "on both paths". A worker who trusts the core expects walk not to fold, and expects `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3` to be computed in floating point. The orientation is presumably the newer text, but the core should agree with it. Confidence medium-low (40%).

2.10 Line 48, `Index`. The paragraph opens "In the library, and in your own generic over such a type, write `I extends Index`", and only near its end limits this to code under walk or checked against the interpreter's library. A worker who acts on the first instruction writes `Index` into a compiled test, which then does not compile. "Walk runs the code without the bound" reads two ways: walk accepts code that leaves the bound out, or walk ignores the bound. Confidence medium-low (40%).

2.11 Line 72. The bold "Only the checker gives a call written as an argument the enclosing call's context" states a departure as the tree's rule, although the next sentences cite walk's behaviour as row 705. I cannot tell whether the rule is "arguments get context, and walk departs" or "only the checker does it". Confidence low-medium (40%).

2.12 Line 109. The bold "A reduction's static argument depends on the path" is a description, not a rule, which goes against line 5 ("Each bold rule states the rule of this tree"). The rule a worker needs is the instruction that follows it: write the static argument of `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN` in every clause form. The file does not say whether a written static argument also directs walk, though "Write it in every clause form" implies it. Confidence low-medium (35%).

2.13 Line 121. "Walk runs it, except in a method that implements an abstract one (row 405)": I cannot tell whether the departure in row 405 is walk running an untyped parameter or walk failing in the implementing method. The list "a function, a method or a local function" leaves out a function expression (`fn x => ...`), which line 70 mentions. Confidence medium-low (45%).

2.14 Line 32, `override`. The file says when an `override` overrides, but not what overriding does under dispatch on every argument. Presumably the wider body then runs at the inherited, narrower types in place of the inherited body. A worker can follow "never Java-style" without being able to predict which body runs. Confidence medium-low (40%).

2.15 Line 91. "...through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` ..., with one result for each place where the numeral is written" reads two ways: the coercion runs once for each written occurrence, or the coercion may give a different result depending on the place. Confidence medium-low (40%).

2.16 Lines 13 and 19: statements made for the checker alone. P-157's substitution of the meet of a parameter's bounds (line 13) and the refusal of `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` (line 19) are stated for the checker, and walk is not mentioned. The bold rule at line 19 suggests that both paths should refuse the duplicate. Confidence low (30%).

2.17 Line 11. The example assumes, without saying so, that `Round` extends `Shape`. "At every instance, not at one only" does not say which instance of one declaration is paired with which of the other. Confidence low (30%).

2.18 Line 24. "An abstract functional method also counts for it": as one of the two overloads that need a cover, or as the cover itself. The example settles the first reading, but the second is not ruled out. Confidence low (30%).

2.19 Line 41, row 695. "A compiled body of `T` that returns `self`" does not say whether the failure is for every such body or only for one whose return type is the parameter `X`, as in `floor(self): I = self`. Confidence low (30%).

2.20 Line 103. It writes `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` operands and `asFloat` for `ZZ64` ones, but leaves out the reason: no coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, which line 99 only implies. A worker who writes `(1.0 s) / n` with `ZZ64` operands cannot predict the result. Confidence low (30%).

2.21 Line 95 against line 89. Walk converts "at a call, a typed binding and an assignment", while line 89's places also include a field and a declared return type. It is unclear whether walk converts there. Confidence low (25%).

2.22 Line 7. "Do not assert it as correct in a test" gives no positive instruction, such as asserting the bold rule and marking the test `XXX`. Confidence low (30%).

2.23 Terms that the core does not give (low, 20-30% each):
- "meet": the core uses it in "a third covers their meet" but defines only "join";
- "the count stage" (line 48): the core names it without defining it;
- `...` in a `comprises` clause (line 38);
- `0#n` (line 107);
- `BIG //` (line 115);
- "extenders" (line 30);
- `HasRank` (line 24), which is glossed only by "make it exclude arrays";
- "route A" and "route C" (line 87): no route B is mentioned, so a reader looks for one.

Placement, which sends no one wrong: tuple and list ordering and `SEQV` (lines 53-62) sit under "Traits and objects", while a reader looking for equality of numbers starts in "Numbers". Line 99's back-reference partly covers this.

## 3. Repair history, or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding

3.1 Line 43, second sentence: "With this reading and the bounds that the test reads ..., the library's generic `+` and `-` between an array and a number are valid beside `AdditiveGroup`'s own." This justifies the library after a checker repair (P-157). A worker who writes a program or a test takes no action from it, and only a checker worker needs it. Keep the two cases where walk still refuses the pair, which do change action, and give them a ledger row (2.3).

3.2 Line 87: "Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again." This is the history of a rejected option. A worker needs only the gloss: route A is flat numbers (P-43), route C a rejected alternative, and "the tower" the number and order traits.

3.3 Line 83: "After the switch-over, such a call still fails, for a second reason. `NatParam` is declared `comprises { N[\n\] } where [\nat n\]`...". This is the mechanism of a future failure. The action is the same now and after the switch-over: run-time sizes are walk-only. The last two sentences (row 307, "This holds for a program's own trait too") change action now, so keep them.

3.4 Line 62: "A float numeral converts where `RR64` is declared ..., so `y: RR64 = 0.5` is `SEQV` `p + p`, computed from `p: RR64 = 0.25`." Both operands are typed `RR64` and `0.25 + 0.25` is exact, so the example teaches nothing beyond "a float by its bits". It reads as a leftover from a time when a typed numeral kept a numeral type. If its point is that a numeral bound at `RR64` is an `RR64` under `SEQV`, one clause does it.

3.5 Line 115: "lifts its elements to `Maybe[\R\]` inside the reduction". This is an implementation mechanism. The actions are to declare `simpleJoin` at `R` and to expect `BIG MAX` to answer `R`, and the lifting changes neither.

3.6 Line 119, first and third sentences ("Walk has no static types", "So walk runs programs that the checker refuses"). These repeat the core, "How a program runs" ("The tree has no static types ... A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed"). Only P-12 and the `Maybe` condition are new.

3.7 Line 109, "Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type". This repeats the core's "Static parameters" bullet. The new parts are "also where the clause form ends a block", the list of places that do not direct it, the fallback to the join, and the message "body param 1".

3.8 Line 66, first and third sentences. These repeat the same core bullet ("takes its bound", "stays open, and every value passes it"). The new parts are the name `OPEN`, the checker's intersection and the three `Bottom` rows.

3.9 Line 13, "By the exclusion rule, a value of both domains has one instance of each generic type at each position, so those instances' static arguments are equal." This is a derivation, and the rule and its two examples carry the action without it. It is borderline: it helps a worker predict untested cases, so it could stay if shortened.

Apart from 3.1 and 3.2, the file carries no repair narrative: no batch, fix or earlier state of the tree is described.

=== README.md
<!-- The orientation workflow: consolidate the fortress-repo skill's revival part into a short orientation every worker reads whole, or update it after a landing from the FACTS the landing changed; how to run it and install its result. -->

# The orientation workflow

The `fortress-repo` skill's revival part, `references/revival-changes.md`, becomes the **orientation**: the short account of how revived Fortress departs from the original and from what a model expects, which every worker reads whole (Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`). `orientation.js` writes it, in two modes:

- **consolidate**, once, and again whenever the part has drifted: an outline by the concepts workers use and a table of where each old entry goes (`outline.md`); the writer writes the whole text from them; a preservation check against the table, a cold read with only the skill's core, and the regression quiz; the writer's fix round; a second cold read and the quiz again; a judge.
- **update**, after every landing: the landing's new and changed FACTS and POSITIONS entries pass the admission test (`admission.md`: the wrong default, the correction, the mistake it prevents); the writer rewrites the sections they touch in place, within the budget of 8K to 12K characters; the same checks, fix round, reread and judge.

The writer is a headless Opus stream (`../record-clarity/writer-stream.sh`), so its fix round resumes the session that wrote the text. The regression quiz is kept in `regression/` (questions and key), and grows with each update.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/orientation.js',
               args: { mode: 'consolidate', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation', concepts: ['/abs/concepts.md'] } })
    Workflow({ scriptPath: ..., args: { mode: 'update', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'orientation-bN', facts: ['F-261', 'P-153'] } })

## Installing its result

The judge writes `judgement.md` and `queue.md`. The coordinator then has the skill writer (`skill-writer.sh`) install the sections judged "install" into `references/revival-changes.md`, add `sources-mapping.md` to the skill's `references/sources.md`, and, after a consolidation, update the core's line for the part and its description together; then a cold read of the installed part, as `coordinator/references/skill-rewrite.md` says. Held sections keep the old text; their items go to `review-queue.md`.

=== admission.md
<!-- The orientation workflow's admission brief, update mode: which findings of a landing earn a place in the orientation. -->

You decide which findings of a landed batch change the `fortress-repo` skill's orientation, in the Fortress revival repository. Change nothing but your report. Commit nothing. Your standard: `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`, "A small change to the existing process" and "Recovered admission rule, workflow runs and transcript search pointers".

Your launch message names the FACTS and POSITIONS entries the landing added or changed. For each (`explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'F-N+'` or `'P-N+'`): does it change what a worker must understand or do? Name the default assumption a worker would hold, the correction for revived Fortress, the consequential mistake it prevents, and the evidence of that mistake (a failure on record, the regression quiz, or the pretraining quiz). If the orientation already states it, or an area part owns it, or no worker would act differently, it is not admitted: say where it belongs instead. Read the skill's current orientation, `.claude/skills/fortress-repo/references/revival-changes.md`, before you decide.

Write `admission.md` in your folder: one row per entry, admitted or not, the reason, and for an admitted one the section it changes. Your structured result: the admitted entries, and a summary.

Read `CLAUDE.md`, the `fortress-repo` skill's core (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`), and the file your launch message names, which is to become the skill's orientation: what a worker must know about revived Fortress before work. Read nothing else. Change nothing but your report. Commit nothing.

Write your report to the path your launch message names:
1. For each section: what would you do differently after reading it? State the rule and its limits without opening any source.
2. Each passage that would send a worker wrong, reads two ways, or uses a term the core does not give, with your confidence.
3. Each passage that holds repair history or detail that changes no action and prevents no misunderstanding (Astra's two questions).

=== judge.md
<!-- The orientation workflow's judge: decide, once, whether the new orientation is installed, section by section. -->

You judge a rewrite of the `fortress-repo` skill's orientation, in the Fortress revival repository. Change nothing but your files in your folder. Commit nothing. Your folder holds `orientation.md` (the final text), the reports on it (`preserve.md`, `cold-read.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, the quiz's grading files) and, by mode, `outline.md` and `disposition.md` or `admission.md`. - **install:** no preservation failure is left, no quiz case fails because of the text, and the second cold read finds nothing that would send a worker wrong.
- **hold:** a section that fails one of these keeps the old text in the skill (in update mode: the change is not made); its failure goes to the review queue.

Write `preserve.md` in your folder: the failures first, each with the old passage, the new one or its absence, and the consequence for a worker; then the count of rows checked. Your final message: its path and the failures, one line each.

=== quiz-author.md
<!-- The orientation workflow's quiz author: the trap questions a worker must answer right, with expected answers from the current record, kept as a regression set. -->

You write the regression quiz for the `fortress-repo` skill's orientation, in the Fortress revival repository. Change nothing but the files named below. Commit nothing. Your standard: `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`, "A small test to preserve through consolidation" and "Operationalize the admission test".

Sources: `explorations/reviews/fortress-pretraining-quiz.md` (what a model believes about Fortress from memory), `explorations/reviews/skills-distillation-audit.md` (its grading, sections A5 and B.10), the record (FACTS and POSITIONS, by `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`), and in update mode the admitted findings (`admission.md` in your folder).

The regression set lives in `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/regression/`: `questions.md` (neutral task questions, numbered, no hints) and `key.md` (for each: the expected decision with its path and scope qualifications, and its evidence). In consolidate mode, write the set: about 12 to 20 questions on consequential wrong assumptions, including how to run a source program, what to do when the specification and an implementation disagree, whether a numeric relation or conversion from another language holds, and one case where the right action is to follow a pointer or explore. Update each old expected answer to the current record; the 2026-10-08 audit is not a timeless oracle. In update mode, add or update only the cases the admitted findings touch, and list the case numbers to run in your folder's `quiz-cases.txt` (in consolidate mode: all).

Your final message: the case count, the cases to run, and any case whose answer the record does not settle.

=== quiz-grade.md
<!-- The orientation workflow's quiz grader: compare the reader's answers with the key. -->

You grade the regression quiz of the `fortress-repo` skill's orientation, in the Fortress revival repository. Change nothing but your report. Commit nothing. Compare the answers file your launch message names with `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/regression/key.md`, case by case: right, wrong, or right without its path or scope qualification. A wrong answer counts against the orientation only if a passage of it misled the reader or a rule the key needs is missing; name which. Write your grading to the path your launch message names. Your final message: the counts, and each failed case with its cause in one line.

=== quiz-reader.md
<!-- The orientation workflow's quiz reader: answer the regression questions with only the skill's core and the new orientation. -->

You are a new worker in the Fortress revival repository (`/home/user/fortress`). Read `CLAUDE.md`, the `fortress-repo` skill's core (`.claude/skills/fortress-repo/SKILL.md`) and its area parts under `references/` (not `revival-changes.md`, not `sources.md`), and the orientation file your launch message names. Then answer the questions in `explorations/coordinator/tools/orientation/regression/questions.md` whose numbers are in the cases file your launch message names. Do not open `key.md` or any other file. For each: your decision, its path and scope, and the passage you relied on. Write your answers to the path your launch message names. Change nothing else. Commit nothing. Your final message: its path.

=== write.md
<!-- The orientation workflow's writer brief: write the orientation from the outline, or update it after a landing. -->

You write the `fortress-repo` skill's orientation, its revival part, in the Fortress revival repository. Your standing order is the skill writer's; here you write into the folder your task names, not into the skill, and commit nothing. Your standard: `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`, its "Consolidation procedure", step 5, and "A small change to the existing process".

Your task names a mode.
- **consolidate:** write `orientation.md` in your folder, whole, from `outline.md` and `disposition.md` there. Give each current rule, the scope and the exceptions needed to apply it, and at most a short contrast with original Fortress or a short example where it prevents a likely mistake. Keep essential path differences (walk and the compiled path) in the orientation itself. Link to the area part for specialist detail. No batch history, no repair chronology: that is `sources.md`'s. Write `sources-mapping.md` too: for each new heading, the old entries it replaces and their source lines.
- **update:** copy the skill's current part into `orientation.md` in your folder, then change it where `admission.md` there says a landed finding changes what a worker must understand: rewrite the existing explanation of that subject in place; add a section only if no section owns it. 3: This part gives the departures of revived Fortress from the team's Fortress, and from what you expect from Java, Scala, Haskell or Julia. The team left three forms that disagree: the specification, walk with the interpreter's library, and the compiled path with the compiler's library. The rules below resolve them. Read the part whole, after `SKILL.md`, before work.
4: 
5: Each bold rule states the rule of this tree. A sentence that names a POSITIONS entry (P-N) states a decision of the curator. Build on a sentence without one, but do not cite it as a decision. Question a rule only on new evidence (`SKILL.md`, "When to explore"). Most rules follow the team's later type papers (`Papers/`) over the specification's early text (P-26; `exploring.md`). The Working Draft is the unrevised specification, in `Specification-1.0-frozen/`. Where a rule changed the specification, Appendix I keeps the original text (`specification.md`).
6: 
7: A sentence that cites a ledger row states a known departure of one path from a bold rule. A fix can change it, so do not assert it as correct in a test. A sentence that opens "Until the switch-over" states a limit of the compiler's library. The limit ends when the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, so do not fix it in the compiler's prelude (`compiler.md`). If a change is not here, search FACTS and POSITIONS (`records.md`) before you call a disagreement a conflict. An old note, a team test and your training can be right about the team's walk and wrong here: the number types do not nest, fixed-width arithmetic does not wrap, and walk converts arguments.
8: 
9: 
10: ## Numbers
11: 
12: **The number types are flat siblings (P-43).** The record calls this choice route A. Route C is the way not chosen: a checker rule under which the number types could nest again. The record still calls the number and order traits "the tower". That word does not mean that they nest.
13: 
14: **A numeral converts where it stands (P-173).** A numeral's own type is `NaturalNumeral`, or `RadixPointNumeral` with a radix point (P-174). Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`, and hold the numeral's exact value. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude names them `IntLiteral` and `FloatLiteral`. A place fixes a type when its declared type is a numeral type, or has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`, and `(h = 0.5)` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when it runs. Walk gives `Infinity` for the second (row 967). Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). A size of 2^31 or more, used as a value, is a `ZZ64` under walk and raises compiled (row 962).
15: 
16: Write a numeral type only as the parameter type of a coercion or an operator. The checker refuses it as the type of a variable, a field or a return (P-174). A program's own number type receives a numeral through its own `coerce(x: NaturalNumeral)` or `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`. Until the switch-over, a compiled program writes `coerce(x: IntLiteral)` or `coerce(x: FloatLiteral)`. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it. Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. Other departures from these rules are rows 958, 960, 966 and 968 under walk, and rows 957, 961, 963, 964 and 965 compiled. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` describe them.
17: 
18: **An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker, on both paths (P-173).** The fold covers the arithmetic operators, `^` up to the exponent 4096, `MIN`, `MAX`, the comparisons and the integer operators such as `DIV`, `REM` and `CHOOSE`. It leaves alone the wrapping, saturating and bitwise operators, the shifts, a division by zero, an integer base at a negative exponent, and a result that can be `-0.0`. A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one numeral, which converts as above or takes its default, and a quotient of integer numerals defaults to a `QQ`. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171), with character literals among them where one of the first two operands is a string. A test of run-time arithmetic or concatenation needs a typed operand: write `m: ZZ32 = 2147483647`, then `m + 1`, or `t: String = "ab"`, then `t || "c"`.
19: 
20: **Arguments convert by declared coercions, and a generic call promotes.** Walk converts a value other than a numeral at a call, a typed binding and an assignment, but not at a declared return type (row 387), and chooses the coercion by the run-time value; the checker chooses it statically (P-59). Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, both paths read the numeral at its default.
21: 
22: **An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).
23: 
24: **`Number` declares nothing (P-165).** Each of the eight number types, and the two numeral types, declares its own `asFloat` into `RR64`. So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. To compare values across types at known types, write `asFloat(x) = y`. In generic code over `T extends Number`, declare your function once for each number type instead. A program may also declare its own number type below `Number` (P-160).
25: 
26: **An integer power answers its base's type (P-153).** In the interpreter's library, `^` takes an exponent of any integer type. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).
27: 
28: **`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

# Working in the Fortress revival repository

The team at Sun Labs built the Fortress language from 2003 to 2012 and left it unfinished. This repository finishes their design from what they left: the code, the specification and the papers. The goal is the model program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.

**curator**
: Person in charge of this restoration.

**brief**
: Instructions that you were launched with. It gives your mission.

**original tree**
: What the team left in this repository: the code, the specification, the papers and their git history. On disk, it is everything outside `explorations/`, `research/`, `CLAUDE.md` and `.claude/`.

**record**
: Project's memory: the files under `explorations/` that hold what the project has established, decided and measured (below).

**walk**
: Interpreter, and the default command of `bin/fortress`: `bin/fortress P.fss` is the same as `bin/fortress walk P.fss`.

**compiled path**
: Other way to run a program: `bin/fortress compile P.fss` writes JVM bytecode, and `bin/fortress run P` runs it.

**model program**
: microGPT, the program by which the revival is measured. It has two programs: the flat program, which the record calls C4 (`explorations/run-c4/src/MicroGptFlat.fss`), and the APL program (`explorations/apl/mg/MicroGptApl.fss`). Each has a quick check beside it, `MicroGptFlatQuick.fss` and `MicroGptAplQuick.fss`. A model line is a source line of either program.

**one library**
: Interpreter's library, which both paths use after the switch-over (below).

**component**
: Unit of Fortress code, in a `.fss` file of its own name. A component implements the apis that it exports, and uses the apis that it imports.

**api**
: Interface, in a `.fsi` file of its own name.

**area**
: One part of the system: the interpreter, the compiled path (the checker, the code generator and the runtime), the library, or the specification.

**base**
: Commit that your work starts from.

**gate**
: Full check of a tree before it lands, when a brief asks for it. To land a tree is to commit it to `main` and push `main`.

**harness**
: Suites' own test runner. Each test is a whole Fortress program, not a JUnit test of a Java class. The harness runs the program and checks the result, as LLVM's lit does for Swift's test suite. `harness-one.sh` and `junit.sh` run it on the files that you name.

**building**
: Normal mode of work where you carry out the mission of your brief. You take the facts and the curator's decisions in the record as given.

**exploring**
: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.

You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.

## How a program runs

Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.

### The phases

Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):

1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
2. Bind each name to its declaration.
3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.

Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled runtime

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

## The record

The record's main files:

- `explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md`: the curator's decisions.
- `explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md`: what is established about the original tree. Each fact names its test and points to the report that holds its detail.
- `explorations/coordinator/INDEX.md`: one line for each note under `explorations/`.
- `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md`, the gap ledger: the known gaps, one row each.

Read a slice of the record with `explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh`. `references/records.md` lists its queries.

## When to explore

Switch from building to exploring when you meet one of these:

- A gap: something missing or broken that the record does not know.
- A conflict: two of the team's sources disagree, and no decision of the curator says which one is correct. The team's sources are the specification, the papers, the library and the implementations.
- New evidence against a decision of the curator. Evidence is new only if the decision did not use it. Your own view of the evidence that it used is not new evidence.

When you switch, load `references/exploring.md`. It says which choices are yours and which go to the curator.

## Rules for every task

- Carry out the curator's decisions as the record states them.
- If the record does not settle a question that your work meets, switch to exploring.
- Cite a source for each claim that you write: your brief, an entry of the record, or a primary source (the code, the specification, the papers or a command's output).
- Reproduce a behaviour before you explain it: run a command that shows it, unless your brief cites the command's output.
- When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause.
- Write the test before the fix for every edit of source code in the original tree. Add the test to the test suite and see it fail through the harness. Then make the fix and see the test pass. An edit of the specification or the documentation has no test (`references/tests-writing.md`).
- Assert every value that matters inside the test, with the harness's own checks (`references/tests-writing.md`), and take the suite's pass or fail as the result. Do not compare the output of a whole run of tests with a saved copy, and do not add expected-output files. The gate's comparisons, and a comparison of outputs that your brief asks for, are the exceptions (`references/gate.md`, "Comparing with an earlier run").
- Take the tree that you start from as passing: its suites passed before it landed. Do not run them to check that. Start with your own failing test.
- Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate, a test or a measurement that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it. Run it again only after the code changes. Running a new program is not a repeat.
- Before you investigate a defect, or edit a file of the original tree, look for its rows in the gap ledger, with the queries of `references/records.md`, "Reading the record".
- After your fix, run your own tests. Run a whole suite where `references/tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite", asks for it, and nowhere else.
- Set up each Bash call as `references/build-and-caches.md` says, because every call starts a new shell.
- After an edit, take the step that `references/build-and-caches.md` gives for the kind of file that you edited.
- Run long commands (a build, a suite) in the background with a log under your tree's `tmp/`, and poll the log (`references/session.md`). Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: if the Bash tool's time limit stops the command, it shows nothing.
- Before you design a change to the library, study how the library already does the same kind of thing, and follow its way (`references/library.md`).
- Do not claim credit for the revival anywhere in a committed file. If git does not record who wrote something, reconstruct the authorship from the history. Do not guess it.
- Commit only the paths that you wrote. Do not commit scratch: logs, captured output, probe programs. Do not rename a file to get it past `.gitignore`. Each agent's transcript keeps how the work was done (`references/committing.md`).
- End your work with a report. List in it the defects that you found, your decisions, and the points that your brief asks for. Put a question for the curator in it as a decision not taken (`references/records.md`).

## The parts

Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words that you need to understand what the query prints.

The parts, in the order that work meets them:

- Setting up each call, building, the caches, what to rebuild after an edit: `references/build-and-caches.md`
- The Bash tool and its timeout, long commands and polling, waits and the prompt cache, stopping processes, interrupts and stops of the session's process, the automatic permission check: `references/session.md`
- The base and its build, worktrees seeded from it, the old code beside the new: `references/worktrees.md`
- The build failing, JDKs, scalac and ASM traps, generated sources: `references/toolchain.md`
- The interpreter area: walk's code (`interpreter/`), where a fix of walk belongs, its checks at load, its natives, running programs under walk, the microGPT check: `references/interpreter.md`
- The compiled area: the checker, the code generator, the runtime, compiled runs, the `fortress` commands, the checker's time after a change: `references/compiler.md`
- The library area (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`): `references/library.md`
- The specification area (`Specification/`), Appendix I, citing it: `references/specification.md`
- How revived Fortress differs from the team's Fortress and from the languages that you know: `references/revival-changes.md`
- Exploring: where to search, what to record and report, which choices are yours: `references/exploring.md`
- Writing a test: `.test` keys, `XXX` expected failures and their promotion, refusals at load, how a defect that you found is recorded: `references/tests-writing.md`
- Running one test, a few, or a whole suite, and when to run a whole suite; what runs outside the gate: `references/tests-running.md`
- The gate: what it runs and writes, the atomic runs, the ladder regression, comparing with an earlier run: `references/gate.md`
- Committing and pushing: `references/committing.md`
- What every report holds and where it goes, findings and points to report; POSITIONS, FACTS and the gap ledger; the queries of the record and when to run each; writing the ledger with `ledger.py`; the repository's history: `references/records.md`
- This cloud platform (the machine, the disk, the network, the platform's stops, the transcript backup, a lost container): the `cloud-container` skill.

A task usually needs several parts. Every task needs `records.md`, for its queries and its report. If a task reads or changes the original tree (its Java and Scala, the library, the tests or the specification), or reviews such a change, read `revival-changes.md` whole, after this file, before work. A task that only runs a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a commit does not need it, until it must read a failing test's source: then read it. For example, a fix of walk needs `revival-changes.md`, `build-and-caches.md`, `session.md`, `worktrees.md`, `interpreter.md`, `tests-writing.md`, `tests-running.md` and `committing.md`. An edit of the library needs the same parts and `library.md`.

`references/sources.md` gives the source of each fact in these parts. Use it only to maintain this skill. Do not load it for a task.

native component FlatString

import String.{maxLeafSize, concatAndBalanceIfNecessary, CatString, spaces}
import Stream.{...}

export FlatString


private language="java"
private package="com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim"

lineSeparator: String = LineSeparator()

private natLineSeparator(): String = builtinPrimitive(
            "com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.lineSeparator")

private LineSeparator(): String =do
    ignore(FlatString); (* This initializes the constructor for FlatString
                   before its type is used (in the next line). *)
    natLineSeparator()
  end

object FlatString extends { String, DelegatedIndexed⟦Char, ZZ32⟧ }
    getter size() : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")
    getter asExprString() : String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.asExprString")
    getter asFlatString(): String = self
    getter asString(): String = self
    getter asDebugString(): String = asDebugStringIndented(0)
    getter depth():ZZ32 = 0

    (* With the help of trait DelegatedIndex, this defines our generate method *)
    getter generator() : Generator⟦Char⟧ =
        self.indices.map⟦Char⟧(fn (i:ZZ32):Char ⇒ self.get(i))

    getter isBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isAlmostBalanced():Boolean = true
    getter isExtremelyUnbalanced():Boolean = false

    balanced():String = self

    opr |self| : ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeStrlen")

    uncheckedSubstring(r1: Range⟦ZZ32⟧) : String = do
    (* We could build a subString node here, but not until everything is working,
        because that will introduce
       SubString objects into code that may still expect FlatStrings.
       As written, this method always answers a FlatString.
       In any case, the FlatString object supports substring without copying*)
        assert((r1 ∩ self.bounds).isEmpty, r1.isEmpty,
                    "Empty substring of non-empty string")
        if r1.isEmpty then ""
        else self.javaSubstr(r1.left.get, r1.right.get + 1)    (* Java substr's endIndex is one past the last character *)
        end
    end

    opr =(self, other: FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.stringEquals")
    opr <(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) < 0
    opr <=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≤ 0
    opr >(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) > 0
    opr >=(self, other: FlatString): Boolean = self.cmp(other) ≥ 0
    opr CMP(self, other: FlatString): TotalComparison =  self.cmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CMP(self, other:String):TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CMP self)
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:FlatString): TotalComparison =
      self.cicmp(other) CMP 0
    opr CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP(self, other:String): TotalComparison = INVERSE (other CASE_INSENSITIVE_CMP self)

    (** get skips bounds checking. **)
    get(i:ZZ32): Char =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.charAt")
    cmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareTo")
    cicmp(other:FlatString): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.compareToIgnoreCase")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32,hi:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaSubstr")
    javaSubstr(lo:ZZ32): String = javaSubstr(lo, self.size)
    javaIndexOf(c:Char): ZZ32 =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.indexOf")
    flatConcat(self, b:FlatString):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenate")
    flatConcat(self, b:Char):String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleConcatenate.nativeConcatenateChar")
    javaRegExpMatches(m:FlatString): Boolean =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpMatches")
    javaRegExpSplit(m:FlatString, i:ZZ32): String =
        builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.stringOps.javaRegExpSplit")

    indexOf(c:Char): Maybe⟦ZZ32⟧ = do
        i = javaIndexOf(c)
        if i = -1 then Nothing⟦ZZ32⟧ else Just⟦ZZ32⟧(i) end
      end

    verify():() = do
        assert(self.depth, 0, self)
    end

    asDebugStringIndented(indent: ZZ32): String =
        spaces(indent) || "J" |self| "/" self.depth ":" self

    opr ∈(c:Char, self): Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ≠ -1

    rangeContains(r: Range⟦ZZ32⟧, c: Char):Boolean = self.javaIndexOf(c) ∈ self.bounds[r]

    (** The operator %||% with at least one String argument converts to string and
        concatenates **)
    opr ||(self, b:FlatString): String = do
        if b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
             (* Since both self and b have depth 0, balancing can't be necessary *)
            CatString(self, b)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end
      end

    opr ||(self, b:String):String = do
        if self.isEmpty then b
        elif b.isEmpty then self
        elif self.size + b.size > maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
        else
            typecase b.asFlatString of
                f:FlatString ⇒ flatConcat(self, f)
                f:String ⇒ concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b)
            end
        end
    end

    opr ||(self, b:Char): String =
        if |self| ≥ maxLeafSize then
            concatAndBalanceIfNecessary(self, b.asString)
        else
            flatConcat(self, b)
        end

    splitWithOffsets():ZeroIndexed⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧ = Nothing⟦(ZZ32, String)⟧
    split():Generator⟦String⟧ = Nothing⟦String⟧

    writeOn(stream: WriteStream): () = stream.write(self)

end FlatString

end

######## P-173
facts-extract: part 1 of 1. Its 1 part prints 3393 bytes, about 1500 tokens.
Asked for, and where it is:
  P-173                                                      POSITIONS.md:104, Numbers  [3060 bytes]

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:104
- P-173 **A numeral converts where it stands: where its place fixes a type, into that type at compile time from its exact value; where nothing fixes one, into the machine default, a `ZZ32`, or a `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, and with a radix point an `RR64`.** A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as the eight number types have and a program's own type may (P-174), or is a numeral type; `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, an unbounded type parameter and no declared type take the default. So `x = 3` is a `ZZ32`, and `x SEQV z` is `true` for `z: ZZ32 = 3`; `bigN = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64` at its binding (row 946). The default applies to a numeral, a literal after the fold, never to an expression of a numeral type, and a `nat` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32` (P-40). A type parameter that several numerals fix takes the narrowest default that holds every value, an `RR64` where any has a radix point, each numeral converting into it exactly; a float numeral whose conversions into `QQ` and `RR64` tie reads `RR64`. At a typed place the conversion is exact or rounds once (P-76, P-172), and a numeral outside the type's range is refused statically; walk converts from the exact value at the same places, place by place, before it runs the checker (P-12). An expression of numerals alone folds exactly before the checker into a signed constant, which defaults as an integer numeral, as a `QQ` for a quotient, or as an `RR64` with a radix point: so `x = 7/2` is a `QQ`, `1/2 = 0.5` is `true`, and `-2147483648`, prefix minus on a numeral, folded, is a `ZZ32`. The library's `=` pairs over the numeral types stay, their conversion of a numeral folded. `gg(5, w)`, with `gg` declared at `(ZZ32, T)` and at `(Any, Any)`, runs the `ZZ32` declaration (P-49). Why: the design completes the Working Draft's, whose numerals have types of their own so that a library decides by coercions how they meet other types (P-174 gives that ground). It bends P-26 in two places, the numeral types' names and the places that fix no type, where the compiler's prelude, the team's later word, keeps the numeral's own type; the curator takes the bend by his right to finish the specification. He declined exact defaults, `ZZ` and `QQ` (the 2012 restart gives `NN` and `QQ`, `literals.tick:25`), since microGPT's untyped hyperparameters (`MicroGptFlat.fss:18`) would then be rationals and every untyped index would need `asZZ32`. What it keeps and changes in form: the judgement's section 3. POSITIONS.md:105
- P-174 **A numeral's own type is the Working Draft's, `NaturalNumeral` or, with a radix point, `RadixPointNumeral`, both below `Numeral`, and its value carries the Draft's four numbers as fields; a program's own number type receives a numeral through its coercion from that type, which the compiler calls once per class, when the class loads.** The four numbers are the digit count `n`, the digits after the radix point `m`, the radix `r`, and the digits read as one integer in that radix `v` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/expressions/literals.tex:83-129`); they are fields of the value, not static parameters of the type, and the Draft's explicit-radix variants and `Literal[\v\]` fold into the radix field. The two types replace the implementations' `IntLiteral` (P-76) and `FloatLiteral` (P-172). A numeral type is written only as a parameter type, of a coercion or an operator, never as a variable's, field's or return type, so the library's `pi` and `e` (`Library/Constants.fsi:16-17`) are `RR64`. A program's type declares the coercion inside itself, such as `coerce(x: RadixPointNumeral)`, and reads the four numbers; the compiler emits the call with the numbers as constants, so a numeral at a program's type denotes one object per site, as a string literal does (P-171): in his words, "Coerce is just invocation of the numeric type constructor that gets the constants from the parser." A program's type with no coercion from the numeral type refuses a numeral. Inside a coercion's body two numeral values compare by their reduced value, so `2.5` and `2.50` are equal there, under `SEQV` too (P-168). Fields cannot make a size static, so the design contradicts the binary chapter's static word width from a numeral's digit count (`Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/binary.tex:1620-1621`, `:1659-1662`), for Appendix I, and drops its `opr ||` with a numeral. Why: the Draft gives numerals types of their own so that "library designers [can] decide how numerals should interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations" (`literals.tex:141-145`), as an interval type should receive `3.1415926535897932384` unrounded (`:135-141`). The team built that coercion under its own names, with the exact value in the numeral ("ZZ32 now coerces IntLiteral as described in the spec", commit `128f313b5b`, 2009), but never the four numbers, and no team word calls the names temporary or final; the design keeps what they built, one type for each kind of numeral with its exact value at the coercion, and adds the Draft's names and numbers. The team's one word on a numeral's value at run time: "IntLiterals should always be transient objects with minimal lifetime" (`compiler/runtimeValues/FIntLiteral.java:21-23`, 2009). A coercion handed a double loses: a bfloat16 type then rounds `1.00390625000000000001` twice, to `0x3F80`, where one rounding gives `0x3F81`. P-173 weighs the bend of P-26.
